segments.text: Here we are at the Pieve di Santa Maria.
I have to admit something.
When I was working on Vicopisano's fortifications, this church had already stood here for centuries.
But I was busy studying the walls, the slopes of the hill, the entrances to the town and everything that might make it safer.
I don't think I gave it the attention it deserved.
Today, at last, I can make up for that.
The church, in the form you see today, dates from the twelfth century.
But its history goes back even further.
It's first mentioned in a document from nine hundred and thirty-four, and from what it says, the church seems to have existed for some time already.
It's the oldest and the principal church among those that stood in the immediate surroundings of Vicopisano.
And it's also the only one built outside the walls.
An interesting choice.
And now, looking carefully for the first time without a defensive system to design, I notice an even more telling detail.
Medieval churches usually had their entrances facing west.
This church, though, faces one of the old gates of the fortified town: Porta Maccioni, later known as Porta della Rocca.
So the façade doesn't simply follow a rule.
It faces directly towards the town and the people coming and going through its walls.
Now take a closer look.
Once again, the stonework is verrucano, but here it doesn't form a tower or a defensive wall.
It's arranged according to the proportions of Pisan Romanesque architecture.
Three doorways below.
Engaged columns and small blind arches.
A two-light window in the centre of the upper section.
Nothing is left to chance.
If you find the church open, I recommend going inside.
The nave and two aisles are divided by twelve granite columns. Some of the capitals and columns come from buildings of Roman times.
Older stones, reused in a new building.
A choice which, as you've probably gathered by now, I thoroughly approve of.
But there's more than architecture inside.
Go to the apse, at the far end of the church, and look for a large group of carved wooden figures.
It's the Deposition, made in the early decades of the thirteenth century.
It shows the moment when Christ's body is taken down from the cross, surrounded by the Virgin Mary, Saint John, Joseph of Arimathea and Nicodemus.
It's one of the few wooden groups of this kind to have survived with almost all its original figures.
Look especially at Christ's body.
It isn't stiff and motionless: it curves as it's lowered from the cross, with a freedom that departs from the more familiar models of the time.
I'm glad I've finally paused at this church and discovered what I overlooked while working in Vicopisano.
Now I understand that a town doesn't live only through the things that defend it.
It lives through the places where people find a sense of belonging, come together and preserve their shared memory.
And speaking of community life, let's head back towards the centre.
We still have two final stops, both in the heart of Vicopisano.
Let's start with the Torri Gemelle, the Twin Towers.
